tasks.name: Traverse graph structure and shortest-hop relationships
Reason about dependencies and dynamic connectivity

concepts.name: Graph model and visited state
concepts.description: Represent entities as vertices and relationships as edges, and track visited/discovered state so cycles do not cause repeated traversal.

concepts.name: BFS shortest path in unweighted graphs
concepts.description: Use a FIFO frontier to discover vertices in nondecreasing number of edges from the source.

concepts.name: DFS structural traversal
concepts.description: Explore one branch deeply before backtracking to reveal reachability, components, and recursive dependency structure.

concepts.name: Directed-cycle traversal state
concepts.description: Distinguish currently active traversal state from fully finished state when detecting back edges in directed graphs.

concepts.name: Topological dependency order
concepts.description: Order a directed acyclic graph so every prerequisite appears before the work that depends on it.

concepts.name: Disjoint-set connectivity
concepts.description: Maintain dynamic connected components under edge additions using find/union operations.

concepts.name: Graph algorithm discrimination
concepts.description: Choose traversal, topological ordering, union-find, or shortest-path methods from graph direction, weight, and query shape.

concepts.name: Dijkstra for non-negative weighted paths
concepts.description: Repeatedly finalize the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance and relax outgoing non-negative edges.

concepts.name: Shortest-path relaxation
concepts.description: Improve a tentative distance when reaching a vertex through a shorter known path and retain predecessor state when path reconstruction is required.

questions.prompt: A microservice may call several downstream services, and a downstream service may be shared by many callers. What data model best captures these relationships?
questions.explanation: The structure is many-to-many rather than a single sequence or strict tree, so vertices plus directed edges form the natural model.
hints: The same downstream service can have multiple incoming relationships.

error_codes.description: The selected model does not naturally represent shared many-to-many dependencies.

choice_feedback.graph: Correct: shared downstream dependencies make this a graph.
choice_feedback.list: A single list cannot represent branching/shared dependencies naturally.
choice_feedback.tree: A strict tree would require every non-root node to have exactly one parent.
choice_feedback.heap: Priority ordering is not the relationship being modeled.

questions.prompt: A traversal explores a graph that may contain cycles. Flag the design that can repeatedly revisit the same cycle forever.
questions.explanation: Without discovery/visited state, traversing a cycle can enqueue or recurse into the same vertices repeatedly.
hints: Imagine A→B→C→A.

error_codes.description: The missing visited/discovery guard was not identified.
A valid graph-traversal step was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Keep a frontier of discovered work
Follow every outgoing edge without recording whether the destination was already discovered
Read each processed vertex's outgoing neighbors
Stop when the frontier is empty

questions.prompt: Every service-to-service edge counts as one hop. You need the minimum number of hops from gateway G to service X. Which method directly matches the objective?
questions.explanation: With equal edge cost, BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing hop count and therefore finds a shortest-hop path.
hints: All edges have the same unit cost.

error_codes.description: The selected method does not most directly exploit equal edge cost for minimum-hop distance.

choice_feedback.bfs: Correct: FIFO levels correspond to hop count.
choice_feedback.dfs: DFS can find a path but not necessarily the minimum-hop one first.
choice_feedback.dijkstra: Dijkstra works with nonnegative weights but is unnecessary when all weights are equal.
choice_feedback.topo: A dependency order does not compute shortest hop count.

choices.label: Depth-first search and stop at the first path

questions.prompt: Graph edges are A→B, A→C, B→D, C→E. Assume neighbors are processed alphabetically. Order BFS visitation from A.
questions.explanation: BFS visits A, then depth-1 vertices B and C, then depth-2 vertices D and E.
hints: Finish the current hop distance before the next.

error_codes.description: The BFS level-order visitation is incorrect.

items.label: A
B
C
D
E

questions.prompt: While detecting a cycle in a directed dependency graph with DFS, which event is direct evidence of a cycle?
questions.explanation: An edge to a vertex still active on the current DFS path is a back edge and proves a directed cycle.
hints: Previously visited and currently active are different states.

error_codes.description: The selected event does not correctly identify a directed DFS back-edge cycle.

choice_feedback.active: Correct: reaching an active ancestor closes a directed cycle.
choice_feedback.finished: A finished vertex may belong to a completed branch and does not itself prove a cycle.
choice_feedback.new: A new vertex is ordinary traversal progress.
choice_feedback.degree: Out-degree alone does not imply a cycle.

choices.label: An edge reaches a vertex currently active on the DFS recursion path
An edge reaches any vertex that was visited at some time in the past
An edge reaches a never-seen vertex
A vertex has more than one outgoing edge

questions.prompt: Which facts justify using BFS to compute the minimum number of dependency hops?
questions.explanation: BFS needs equal/unit edge cost for hop-count optimality, and FIFO frontier order processes all distance-d vertices before distance d+1.
hints: Why is first discovery optimal?

error_codes.description: Part of the BFS shortest-hop justification was missed.
An unnecessary or incompatible graph property was selected.

evidence.label: Each dependency edge counts as exactly one hop
FIFO frontier processes smaller hop distances first

questions.prompt: A security tool models account-to-account delegation as an unweighted directed graph and must report the fewest delegation steps from account A to account B. Which strategy fits?
questions.explanation: The objective is minimum edge count, so BFS with visited/discovered state is the direct fit.

error_codes.description: The selected strategy does not most directly compute minimum unweighted delegation hops.

choice_feedback.bfs: Correct: each delegation edge contributes one step.
choice_feedback.dfs: DFS may encounter a longer path first.
choice_feedback.uf: Union-find can answer connectivity but not directed shortest-hop path length.
choice_feedback.dijkstra: It works with unit weights but adds unnecessary priority machinery.

choices.label: BFS from A with discovered/visited state
DFS and stop at the first path to B
Dijkstra despite every edge having equal cost

questions.prompt: A deployment plan says database migration must finish before API deploy, and API deploy must finish before smoke tests. Which graph operation produces a valid execution order?
questions.explanation: These are directed prerequisite edges. If the dependency graph is acyclic, a topological order places every prerequisite before its dependent.
hints: The requirement is precedence, not shortest path.

error_codes.description: The selected algorithm does not directly produce prerequisite-respecting order.

choice_feedback.bfs: BFS levels from one source do not necessarily satisfy all DAG prerequisites.
choice_feedback.uf: Connectivity membership does not produce dependency order.

questions.prompt: A build system claims it can produce a complete topological order even when A depends on B, B depends on C, and C depends on A. Flag the incorrect claim.
questions.explanation: A directed cycle makes the precedence constraints contradictory: each task would need to appear before another task in the same cycle, so no complete topological order exists.
hints: Try placing A, B, and C in any linear order while respecting all three edges.

error_codes.description: The impossible-cycle topological-order claim was not identified.
A valid dependency-order step was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Model 'must happen before' as directed edges
Detect whether a directed cycle exists
If a cycle exists, still return some complete ordering and call it topological
If acyclic, return an order respecting all edges

questions.prompt: Network links are activated over time. After each activation, the system frequently asks whether device X and Y are now in the same connected component. The actual path is not needed. Which structure fits?
questions.explanation: This is dynamic connectivity under edge additions: union the endpoints of each new link and compare representatives for connectivity queries.
hints: The operations are repeated union + same-component queries.

error_codes.description: The selected method does not most directly match repeated edge-addition connectivity queries.

choice_feedback.uf: Correct: union/find directly matches the query pattern.
choice_feedback.bfs: Repeated BFS can answer connectivity but repeats traversal work after every link change.
choice_feedback.dijkstra: Weighted shortest paths are not requested.
choice_feedback.topo: The graph is about undirected connectivity, not prerequisite order.

choices.label: Run a fresh BFS from X after every query

questions.prompt: A system uses union-find and now needs the exact shortest sequence of links from device A to device B. What is the key limitation?
questions.explanation: Union-find maintains component membership, not path structure or shortest-route information. A traversal/path algorithm is needed when the route itself matters.
hints: Connected? and 'which route?' are different outputs.

error_codes.description: The selected statement does not identify union-find's path-information limitation.

choice_feedback.path: Correct: union-find does not preserve the shortest path sequence.
choice_feedback.same: Same-component queries are exactly what it is good at.
choice_feedback.rep: Representatives are part of the method, not the limitation described.

choices.label: Union-find does not directly store or return the shortest path between members
Union-find cannot answer whether two vertices are connected
Union-find has no representative element for a component

questions.prompt: An offline batch receives pairs of employee IDs indicating newly merged access groups. After each merge it needs to answer many 'same group?' queries, but never asks for a route between employees. Which data structure best matches?
questions.explanation: The workload is repeated unions plus component-membership queries, so disjoint-set union directly matches it.

error_codes.description: The selected strategy does not best match repeated component-union membership queries.

choice_feedback.uf: Correct: union/find is built for exactly these operations.
choice_feedback.bfs: Repeated traversal is unnecessary when only component identity is needed.

choices.label: Fresh BFS for every same-group query

questions.prompt: A service graph assigns each call edge a non-negative latency estimate. You need minimum TOTAL estimated latency from service A to service Z. Which algorithm directly matches?
questions.explanation: Edge weights matter and are non-negative, so Dijkstra's minimum tentative-distance frontier is the direct fit.
hints: Minimum hop count and minimum weighted latency are different objectives.

error_codes.description: The selected method does not directly minimize total non-negative edge weight.

choice_feedback.dijkstra: Correct: it minimizes total non-negative edge weight.
choice_feedback.bfs: BFS minimizes number of edges, not total latency when weights differ.
choice_feedback.topo: A topological order alone does not solve general weighted shortest paths.
choice_feedback.uf: Union-find answers connectivity, not minimum route cost.

choices.label: BFS treating every call as equal cost

questions.prompt: A graph contains an edge with weight -8. Flag the claim that is unsafe for standard Dijkstra.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's finalization proof relies on non-negative edge weights. A negative edge can later create a cheaper path to a vertex that looked final earlier.
hints: Ask what prevents a later route from reducing an already-selected distance.

error_codes.description: The invalid negative-edge Dijkstra assumption was not identified.
A valid shortest-path setup step was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Read edge weights as path costs
Use standard Dijkstra and assume the first finalized distance can never improve despite negative edges

questions.prompt: Current distances are `dist[A]=4`, `dist[B]=12`. Edge A→B has weight 3. What should relaxation do?
questions.explanation: The route through A costs 4+3=7, which improves B from 12 to 7. Update B's distance and predecessor if path reconstruction is needed.
hints: Compare the current best for B with dist[A] + weight(A,B).

error_codes.description: The selected action does not apply shortest-path relaxation correctly.

choice_feedback.update: Correct: 7 is a strictly shorter known route than 12.
choice_feedback.final: One successful relaxation does not by itself prove B is globally finalized.

choices.label: Set `dist[B]=7` and declare B permanently finalized immediately regardless of queue state

questions.prompt: Which facts justify replacing `dist[v]` during relaxation of edge `u→v`?
questions.explanation: The known route to u plus the edge weight produces a candidate route to v. Replace dist[v] only if that candidate is strictly better than the best known distance.
hints: An update should represent a real path and improve the current best.

error_codes.description: Part of the relaxation-update condition was missed.
A property unrelated to relaxation correctness was selected.

evidence.label: `dist[u] + weight(u,v)` is a valid candidate path cost to v
That candidate is smaller than the current `dist[v]`
v must be the oldest discovered vertex
v must have smaller out-degree than u

questions.prompt: A shortest-path service must return the ACTUAL route, not only its total cost. What extra state should be updated when a relaxation improves vertex v?
questions.explanation: Store the predecessor that produced the improved distance. Following predecessor links backward from the destination reconstructs the chosen path.
hints: You need to remember which previous vertex produced each best route.

error_codes.description: The selected state does not preserve enough information to reconstruct the shortest path.

choice_feedback.prev: Correct: predecessor state records the route tree.
choice_feedback.degree: Degree does not record which edge produced the shortest route.
choice_feedback.visited: Visited/finalized status alone cannot reconstruct the path.
choice_feedback.sorted: Sorting vertex IDs does not encode route choices.

choices.label: `predecessor[v] = u` for the successful improving edge
A sorted list of all vertex IDs

questions.prompt: A heap-based Dijkstra implementation pushes a new `(distance, vertex)` pair every time a better route is found. Why can old heap entries be ignored when their distance no longer equals the best known `dist[vertex]`?
questions.explanation: An older larger heap entry reflects a route that has already been improved. The distance map holds the current best known state; processing the stale larger entry cannot create a better basis than the current smaller one.
hints: The heap may contain history; the distance map is the current best state.

error_codes.description: The selected reason does not explain why an outdated larger heap entry is safe to skip.

choice_feedback.stale: Correct: the outdated pair no longer represents the best known route to that vertex.
choice_feedback.sorted: A heap is not globally sorted.
choice_feedback.negative: Stale entries are not a negative-edge issue.

choices.label: The old pair represents a worse superseded route than the current distance map
Because every heap entry is globally sorted forever
Because stale entries imply negative edges
Because the priority queue behaves like a FIFO queue

questions.explanation: Dijkstra handles non-negative weighted shortest paths; successful relaxations should also update predecessors so the final transition sequence can be reconstructed.
